sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
To efficiently scavenge the energy from low-frequency ambient vibrations, this paper proposed a piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) with a six-segment folded trapezoidal beam. The new configuration provides the PEH with a lower natural resonant frequency and closer resonance peaks, which makes the harvester suitable to daily vibrations with more functioning resonance modals. Meanwhile, the folded geometry extends the whole length of beam, and then induce a larger strain in the clamped end, leading to a more favorable output voltage. The experimental results show that the proposed structure obtains 5 resonant peaks in $0 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and an operating bandwidth of $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The highest open-circuit output voltage is $2 0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V }$ , and the optimized output power is $2 1 7 . 2 0 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ .

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The rapid development of wireless technology provides a lot of convenience to people’s work and life, such as the sensor for detecting subsurface soil moisture and salinity in agriculture and the global positioning system for tracking wildlife.1,2 The biggest problem with the practicality of these wireless systems is the limitation of power supplies. With the help of self-powered devices, the energy from an ambient environment can be an available proposal to satisfy the power demand.3–6 Among them, piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) has been widely used because of its good mechanical-electrical conversion performance and simple structure.7–9 The energy collection efficiency reaches to its maximum value at the resonant frequencies of PEH, but drops sharply once the vibration goes out of this frequency.10,11 To pursue the high conversion efficiency, the low resonant frequency and broad bandwidth corresponding to the target vibrations are required, which can be realized by multi-modal configurations and structural nonlinearity.

The multi-modal scheme for band extension can be applied by various ways. For example, Ferrari et $a l . ^ { 1 2 }$ utilized the cantilever beams with different equivalent mass to construct a wideband energy acquiring array, in which every beam performed as an independent unit with different resonant frequencies. Although the system bandwidth was promoted, only the first mode of every beam was used, and the system complexity was obviously increased by the enlargement of the beam number. Wu et $a l . ^ { 1 3 }$ controlled the first two structural resonant frequencies to the same order by the combination of the main beam and the inner beam, which provided an additional resonant peak to the device without increasing the structural volume. Wang et al.14 constructed a PEH based on the linear multidegree of freedom principle, and successfully reduced the first four resonant frequencies to $2 2 . 9 \ \mathrm { H z } ,$ , $6 3 . 4 ~ \mathrm { H z } ,$ $^ { 9 6 . 8 \ \mathrm { H z } }$ and $2 1 9 \ \mathrm { H z } ,$ which could be attributed to the application of the low-elastic-modulus transmission beam and the traditional metal functioning beam. However, the enhancement just worked well at the first resonant frequency point, and the others still could not be effectively used. In Ref. 15, an M-type beam structure was proposed, which consisted of a main beam and two folded auxiliary beams. The M-type beam structure ensured that the first three natural frequencies were close enough to obtain three resonant points in the frequency of $1 3 { - } 2 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , but the power density was not ideal.

Another way to broaden the bandwidth is to introduce a nonlinearity force into PEHs. In Ref. 16, the upper and lower surfaces of each piezoelectric cantilever are impacted by the attractive and repulsive magnetic forces, respectively. This feature is achieved by two pairs of magnets mounted on the top and bottom of the piezoelectric cantilever beam array. In this structure, the self-resonant frequency tunability of the structure is realized by utilizing the magnetic stiffness technique. In Ref. 17, a primary beam, an inner beam, a spring, and two magnetic masses were utilized to construct a 3D PEH. The two beams with end-mounted magnets can capture vibrations along their surface normal direction. The spring acts as a mechanical energy buffer to sense the vibrations parallel to the length direction of the inner beam. The two structures have one common disadvantage: once the devices are not accurately assembled or unrecoverable deformation happens to the beams after long usage, there may be a significant impact on the output efficiency, and even a loss of the nonlinear state. There are also other ways to conducting nonlinear constructions. For example, in Ref. 18, a cantilever beam with a pendulum ball at its free end was proposed, and the nonlinear coupling was induced by the resonant pendulum movement in three-dimensional space. This proposal can provide the PEH with a large bandwidth and the capability of collecting vibration energy in multiple directions. However, this structure sometimes does not work as expected. So its output power is unstable.

Generally, the frequency of the vibration source of the environment is relatively low, which requires that the vibration energy harvester have the character of wider bandwidth and low resonant frequency .19,20 A lot of design which only focuses on one aspect and ignores the others is the vibration energy harvester is presented in Ref. 20 without using a cantilever beam. There, the researchers used a complex process to produce a proof mass and then, they fixed the proof mass with two cantilever beams on the frame of the collector. This structure not only provides a greater degree for underlying response but also the first three natural frequencies are controlled within the ambient vibration frequency range. However, the fabrication process of this kind of structure is complex, the processing cost is large, and there are only three available resonant points.

To improve the energy conversion efficiency, this paper presents a PEH with a beam folded into six trapezoidal segments. In the proposed structure, the beam can move in more than one direction, and the role of different segments in structural equivalent mass and stiffness varies due to the specially organized configuration, thereby reducing the resonant frequencies. Because of the structural characteristics of the multi-segment beam, there are several resonant modes available for the proposed structure. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, the design and analysis of the new PEH are presented, in which the finite element simulation and comparison are conducted. Section $\mathrm { I I I }$ describes the experimental setup for device characterization, and the results are given and analyzed with a brief discussion. Finally, Sec. $\mathrm { I V }$ summarizes this paper.

sections.heading: A. Design
sections.text:
The proposed PEH is illustrated in Fig. 1, which consists of three parts: a folded cantilever beam, a piezoelectric plate near the clamped end, and a proof mass at the free end. The cantilever beam is made of copper and folded into six segments with the same geometry. The original beam is shown in Fig. 1(a), and the creases are indicated by dashed lines. Every beam segment features a trapezoidal geometry and their dimensions are shown in the inset. A protruding rectangular portion is added to the first-segment as the clamping end to fix the whole device to the fixture. To realize the six-segment folded trapezoidal configuration, the original beam is folded along the dashed lines, and the obtained model is shown in Fig. 1(b) with the definition of each segment. When excited by a vibration, the folded beam will be involved in a bending movement, and the corresponding stress will concentrate in the clamped region, where the piezoelectric plate is placed. Since the structural equivalent mass and stiffness are specially optimized, a relative low working frequency and broad functioning band can be realized. Also, undesired gravity-induced deformation can be avoided by this delicate configuration.

![](images/e04c47c73bae1ca8d6805042044c9482af37fc9b30f8cd18619c6bb840e09466.jpg)  
FIG. 1. (a) Schematic of the original beam and (b) the six-segment folded trapezoidal beam.

![](images/0ad3e5f370ade2ee6e5aa4f60a721a5c5427c488a096d38ce1944f40b56d9b34.jpg)

sections.heading: C. Simulation
sections.text:
Detailed analyses for the proposed structure are conducted by finite element (FE) simulations, and a series of comparisons are also performed to promote and verify the design. The parameters of involved materials are given in Table I, and the dimensions of piezoelectric plate (PZT-5Y) and mass (Fe) are set as $2 2 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 1 9 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ $\times 0 . 3 5 \mathrm { m m }$ (length $\times$ width $\times$ thickness) and $1 8 \mathrm { m m } \times 9 \mathrm { m m } \times 4 \mathrm { m m }$ (l $\mathrm { \ e n g t h { \times } w i d t h { \times } t h i c k n e s s } )$ , respectively.

First, the effect of folding on the structure resonant frequency is investigated by harmonic response analysis, in which the exciting acceleration is $0 . 5 \ { \tt g }$ $( \mathbf { g } = 9 . 8 ~ \mathrm { m } \bar { / } \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } )$ . The used models are illustrated in Fig. 3. The model shown in Fig. 3(a) is the elementary unit for the proposed structure; the trapezoid with $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ in height, $2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ in upper side width, and $5 0 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ in lower side width. The structures in subsequent figures [Figs. 3(a) and 3(b)] are constructed by jointing certain numbers of the basic one. The dashed line in Fig. 3(c) is the place of folding. Under the stimulated acceleration of $_ { 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g } }$ acceleration in the frequency range of $0 { - } 3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , the response characters of different models are simulated and the results are shown in Fig. 4. Then, a static analysis is carried out to investigate the stress distribution at the clamped ends of different structures under a constant acceleration of $0 . 5 \ { \mathrm { g } } { \mathrm { . } }$ , and Fig. 5 illustrates the obtained results.

![](images/0cb9530910da86915aa9c9cd0549b21a8b221fcefb3425e4449a773cfbec2b89.jpg)  
FIG. 3. The schematic for comparison simulation: (a) one-segment cantilever beam, (b) two-segment cantilever beam, and (c) four-segment cantilever beam.

![](images/cadc0e80498202f626088235469dcea21bf2af72c3db1c7f4caac1551f069c9e.jpg)  
FIG. 4. Simulated resonant frequencies of different structural models.

Combining the above two simulation results, it is can be seen that as the structure segment increases, the resonance frequencies of different orders become lower and lower, and the circumstance is more apparent for the structure with more segments. Moreover, the maximum equivalent stresses at the clamped ends, where the piezoelectric plate is located, increase with increasing number of segments. If the segment of folded beam continues to increase, it may generate better simulation data.21 However, it is not very practicable to realize a structure with more than six segments. When the number of folded beam is greater than six, the structure is gradually deformed and internal collision will happen under the applied vibration. Comprehensive consideration of structural performance and realistic realization show that a six-segment folded cantilever beam has more advantages.

Then, the influence from segment geometry is simply simulated. A folded beam with six rectangular segments is modeled as the reference structure. The comparison of segments between the rectangular beam and the trapezoidal beam is shown in Fig. 6. The simulation result is shown in Fig. 7. It can be found that both structures effectively control their first nine natural resonant frequencies in the range of $0 { - } 1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Obviously, the natural resonant frequencies of the trapezoidal structure are lower than those of the rectangular structure. Meantime, the first five resonant frequencies of the trapezoidal structure are all below $3 0 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ and their distribution is more concentrated than that of the rectangular structure.

sections.heading: III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
sections.text:
The experimental setup is shown in Fig. 8. The generated sine wave signal with different frequencies are amplified and then transmitted to the exciter, by which the target vibration is applied to the PEH. The accelerometer monitors the applied acceleration of the exciter and its output is transmitted to the oscilloscope. Finally, the output voltage of the PEH is observed by an oscilloscope. The experimental device is shown in Fig. 9.

The acceleration of the exciter is adjusted to $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g } ,$ and the open-circuit output voltage of the proposed configuration is tested.

![](images/92cc72d85fa617283e89e3e874e13804b7d18982a368f7fefb31f986176112b8.jpg)  
FIG. 5. Stress distribution of different structural models: (a) one-segment cantilever beam, (b) two-segment cantilever beam, (c) four-segment cantilever beam, and (d) six-segment cantilever beam.

The amplitude and frequency response is shown in Fig. 10. It can be seen that the structure resonates at $3 . 6 \mathrm { H z } , 7 . 1 \mathrm { H z } .$ , $1 3 . 2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 5 . 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , and $2 8 \mathrm { H z }$ , and the corresponding peak voltages are $2 0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V }$ , $1 5 . 4 5 \mathrm { V }$ , $8 . 4 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , $5 . 3 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , and $5 . 6 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively. The bandwidth is about $1 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ from $0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ to $3 0 \ \mathrm { H z } .$ , among which the current is greater than $2 . 5 \mu \mathrm { A }$ and the voltage is above $3 \mathrm { V }$ . It is large enough to drive diodes in the rectification circuit. Because the first and second beams are on the same plane, the first two resonant points are closer than the second and third ones. Moreover, the resonant frequency obtained by the experiment is generally smaller than the simulated ones, which can be attributed to the deviation between the damping coefficient appearing in simulation and experiment.

Then, we test the output power of the device at the first five resonant peaks, and the power-load resistance curve can be found in Fig. 11. The best matching load resistance at $3 . 6 \mathrm { H z } ,$ , 7.1 Hz, $1 3 . 2 \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 5 . 5 \mathrm { H z } ,$ and $2 8 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ are $4 9 7 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $2 9 6 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $1 4 8 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $1 2 6 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and $8 5 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , respectively; the corresponding output power are $2 1 7 . 2 0 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ , $2 0 1 . 5 9 6 \mu \mathrm { W } _ { ; }$ , $1 2 1 . 4 7 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ , $5 7 . 0 0 4 \mu \mathrm { W } ,$ , and $9 2 . 2 3 5 \mu \mathrm { W }$ , respectively. Every peak output power of this structure can drive microwireless sensor network nodes.

Finally, the proposed device was excited by vibrations in more directions to evaluate its performance in harvesting multi-direction energy. A $_ { 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g } }$ excitation in the frequency of $0 { - } 1 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ was, respectively, applied along $\mathbf { X }$ and y axes as shown in Fig. 12. It can be seen from the frequency-voltage curve that when the structure is excited in the $\mathbf { X }$ axis, two resonance points at $1 . 4 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $5 . 7 \mathrm { H z }$ are generated, and the corresponding voltages are $9 . 7 6 \mathrm { V }$ and $1 2 . 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ . Then for y-axis vibration, the resonance points appear at $3 . 8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 2 . 9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ with the corresponding voltages of $1 1 . 9 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and $7 . 2 8 \mathrm { V }$ , respectively. Moreover, the simulation results show that the resonant frequency of the proposed structure is $1 . 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and $4 . 7 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ when excitation was applied along the $\mathbf { X }$ axis and the resonant frequency is $3 . 8 \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 2 . 9 \mathrm { H z }$ along the y axis. The difference between simulation and experimental is within the tolerance scope. Benefiting from the multiaspect structural configuration, the proposed prototype exhibits favorable performances in resonant frequency, bandwidth, and multiple-direction harvesting.

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: In this paper, a novel low-resonant and broadband piezoelectric energy harvester is presented. A working beam with six trapezoidal segments is adopted to capture the to-be-harvested vibration, and necessary finite element analysis are conducted to verify the structural properties. The proposed configuration has a wider bandwidth and a lower resonant frequency than the traditional cantilever beam structure, and the utilized trapezoidal beam geometry further lowers the resonant frequency. The experimental results show that the proposed PEH can generate a peak open-circuit output voltage of $2 0 . 7 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ with the maximum output power of $2 1 7 . 2 0 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ when it is excited by a $_ { 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g } }$ sinusoidal acceleration. Moreover, this PEH can also collect vibrational energy from multiple directions. Further structural optimization and possible practical applications will be conducted in the future work.
